subtitle: The Full-Scale Maquette as Prelude to Venice
lede: In preparation for Biennale Arte 2026, <hl>Zadik Zadikian</hl> is developing a full-scale maquette of a new sculptural variation titled <hl>Blue Yellow Blue Yellow</hl>.
p1: This is not a miniature study. It is a one-to-one rehearsal of structure, proportion, and chromatic rhythm—an architectural test before the casting of plaster and the final realization of form within <hl>The Studio</hl>, the Armenian Pavilion’s living atelier.
p2: At its core, the work investigates reflection and repetition. A square side—precise, disciplined, elemental—is mirrored at each successive step upward along the chain of units. The geometry does not simply stack; it responds. Each level echoes the one beneath it, producing a visual cadence: blue, yellow, blue, yellow. Structure becomes rhythm. Form becomes sequence.
p3: Like a musical phrase in a minor key, it advances through modulation rather than spectacle.
h2-cnc: Precision as Foundation: CNC Milling the Foam Core
p4: The maquette begins not with plaster, but with foam. Each unit is CNC-milled to exact dimensions, ensuring structural integrity and repeatability. Precision at this stage is critical.
p5: The foam core will ultimately live inside the plaster shell, reducing weight while maintaining mass and stability—an approach central to <hl>The Studio’s</hl> material language.
p6: This method allows the sculptures to appear monumental while remaining maneuverable—an essential condition for a Pavilion that will assemble, disassemble, and reassemble structures continuously over seven months.
p7: Repetition demands accuracy. Without mathematical rigor, rhythm collapses.
p8: The next phase will flesh out the chromatic body of the work. Blue and yellow are not surface decoration; they are structural forces.
p9: In Zadikian’s practice, pigment is conceived as something incarnated within material rather than applied externally. Even in this maquette stage, color testing is essential. Saturation, edge clarity, and the dialogue between planes must be resolved before casting begins.
blue: Blue carries depth and receding space.
p10: Together, they generate tension. The repetition of the pair stabilizes that tension into pattern.
p11: For decades, Zadikian’s work has operated at the intersection of Minimalist discipline and metaphysical resonance. As Carlo McCormick writes, his practice rises <it>“like a visual song… to that which remains immutable in the seas of change.”</it>
p12: The full-scale maquette is part of that discipline. It is a laboratory of proportion, a site where reflection, stacking logic, and chromatic sequencing are tested under real conditions. Nothing is simulated. Every edge matters. Every angle carries consequence.
p13: Only after this stage will full plaster casting begin.
p14: This work will eventually enter the ecosystem of <hl>The Studio</hl>—a space conceived as an active site of fabrication, touch, arrangement, and re-arrangement.
p15: There, units will not remain fixed. They will shift, recombine, and evolve over time. The square reflected upward in <hl>Blue Yellow Blue Yellow</hl> anticipates that larger logic: continuity through repetition, variation through structure.
closing: In the discipline of repetition, change begins.
